summary: Defines SMTP and MIME extensions that let a message originator state whether content may be converted, for example from colour to black and white, along the way. This allows conversion to be done conveniently in a store-and-forward mail environment. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Suppose you send a colour picture to a friend whose printer only prints black and white. This memo lets mail systems change the picture along the way, if you allowed it, so it still works for them.

questions: how to convert email content in transit
how does email content conversion work
subtitle: How mail servers along the way can convert a message into a form the recipient can handle, with the sender's permission.

tldr.problem: A sender may use a content form the recipient cannot process, or one of higher quality than the recipient wants. Sending every form, or asking the recipient by email first, is slow and unreliable.
tldr.mechanism: Two SMTP extensions, CONPERM (the sender's permission) and CONNEG (the recipient's capabilities), plus three MIME header fields (Content-Convert, Content-Features, Content-Previous) let an intermediary convert the content and record what it did.
tldr.outcome: Conversion is limited to what the originator allows and what the target can take. Signed or encrypted content generally cannot be converted, and the RFC calls the mechanism a significant resource and risk burden for intermediaries.

today: RFC 4141 is a Proposed Standard (November 2005). The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Convert Content in Transit
sections.content:
MIME labels different kinds of content, but an email originator cannot know whether a recipient can handle a particular data type. RFC 3297 lets an originator ask the recipient about its capabilities by exchanging email messages. The RFC notes that this end-to-end exchange adds considerable latency and some unreliability.

RFC 4141 takes another approach. The originator sends the "best" form of the data it can, together with descriptors of acceptable alternatives. The recipient, or an intermediary (an ESMTP host along the path), then converts the content to a form the recipient supports. It builds on the RFC 2912 way of describing media features.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking your friend what they can read before you send anything, you send your best version and let the mail system fix it up on the way.

sections.title: The Moving Parts and Their Limits
sections.content:
The service combines two ESMTP extensions and three MIME header fields. The originator expresses preferences in Content-Convert. CONPERM raises those preferences from advice to a requirement. CONNEG lets a server report what the target can receive. Content-Previous and Content-Features record what was converted and what the content now looks like.

Advice versus requirement matters for failure handling. The RFC's failure table bases the outcome only on the originator's direction: if the originator only advised, the original content is delivered; if the originator required conversion and it could not be done, the message is returned without delivery. The recipient's wishes guide the conversion details, not delivery.

The Applicability section warns that conversion can place significant resource requirements on intermediaries, that an intermediary accepts responsibility before knowing whether it can convert, and that digitally signed or encrypted content cannot be converted unless the intermediary can decode and re-code it.
sections.eli5: The sender can say "please fix it if needed" or "fix it or send it back." The friend's wishes only decide how it is fixed, never whether the letter is delivered.

sections.title: How Originators, Intermediaries and Recipients Act
sections.content:
An originator who includes Content-Convert must also include a Content-Features field describing the current form. Intermediaries MAY treat Content-Convert as authorization to convert. On its own it is only advisory. With CONPERM, conversions MUST be limited to those listed, and if a needed, authorized conversion cannot be done, the message is returned to the originator.

A server that knows the target's capabilities MAY offer CONNEG. When the next hop offers CONNEG during CONPERM handling, the client MUST request the capability information, MUST perform the needed conversion if possible, and MUST fail the message with status code 5.6.5 (Conversion failed) if any conversion fails. The conversions allowed are the intersection of three lists: those the originator permits, the target's capabilities, and what the client host can actually do.

When recipients differ, the intermediary MAY make one copy that suits all of them, or several copies sent in separate SMTP sessions to subsets of recipients. If the next hop supports neither CONPERM nor CONNEG, the client MUST end the session without sending and return a notification with status code 5.6.3 (Conversion required but not supported).
sections.eli5: A post office worker may only change the letter in ways the sender listed, that the receiver can read, and that the worker knows how to do. If that list is empty, the letter goes back or goes on as it was, depending on what the sender asked for.

sections.title: The CONPERM and CONNEG Extensions
sections.content:
CONPERM (Content-Conversion-Permission) is an EHLO keyword. The client adds a CONPERM parameter, with no arguments, to MAIL FROM. If the server did not advertise 250-CONPERM and the client is taking part in CONPERM, the client MUST treat the transmission as permanently rejected. A server that does not support the parameter MUST reject the command with a 504-CONPERM reply.

CONNEG (Content-Negotiation) adds a CONNEG parameter, with no arguments, to RCPT TO. If a message is subject to CONPERM and the server advertises 250-CONNEG, the client MUST use it. Otherwise it MAY. The capability listing comes back as a multi-line reply: each line begins 250-CONNEG except the last, which is 250 CONNEG. The listing follows the feature-set syntax of RFC 2533 and the range permitted in RFC 3297. A server MAY list a broader set than the recipient supports, if what is delivered can still be processed by the recipient.

Having made the request, the client MUST honor the capabilities returned and convert if the current form is not among them. If it converts, it SHOULD pick the "highest" level of capability, a judgment left to the converting host.
sections.eli5: CONPERM is the sender stamping the envelope "you may change this." CONNEG is the next post office saying what the receiver can read. Both are just extra words added to the normal mail conversation.

sections.title: The Three MIME Header Fields
sections.content:
Content-Features describes the current form of a MIME body-part and is specified in RFC 2912. There is one per body-part.

Content-Convert gives the permitted conversions: ANY, NONE, or an explicit list of acceptable final forms. With ANY the intermediary may do whatever it deems appropriate. With NONE it SHOULD NOT convert, even when the target cannot handle the original. The field MUST be carried unmodified to the recipient. Without it, intermediaries SHOULD NOT convert.

Content-Previous records a conversion: a Date (when it was converted), a By (the domain of the intermediary) and the earlier form. An intermediary MUST add it, and MUST create or revise Content-Features to describe the result. The RFC notes that a chain of conversions can lose more information than necessary, for example if converting A to B and then B to C is worse than converting A directly to D.
sections.eli5: The converted letter carries sticky notes: one says what it looks like now, one says what it used to look like, who changed it and when, and the sender's note says what changes were allowed.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's examples use a fax-over-email setting (the server banner is IFAX) with TIFF-FX content. In the CONPERM example the client sends MAIL FROM with CONPERM and the message carries a Content-Convert field that lists acceptable forms such as image coding JBIG, paper size letter or A4, and resolution of 204, 200 or 400 dpi.

In the CONNEG example the client adds CONNEG to RCPT TO and the server answers with a series of 250-CONNEG lines describing what the recipient can take. A Content-Previous example shows the date Tue, 1 Jul 2001 10:52:37 +0200, the converting domain relay.example.com, and the prior form of the content.
sections.eli5: The examples show a fax machine on email telling the sender "I can print A4 or letter paper," and a mail relay noting down what it changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The service discloses recipient capabilities. How the requester and responder are authenticated is outside the specification, and the disclosed information is meant to be safe for public distribution. If something needs restricted distribution, the disclosing ESMTP server or client must decide whether extra protection is needed.

Encrypted content cannot be converted, because the intermediary is not expected to have the keys. Signed but unencrypted content is invalidated by conversion. The RFC also warns that conversion means potentially unbounded computation by intermediaries, which could open a denial-of-service opportunity, and that using unspecified intermediaries "carries significant risk". It argues that the mechanism is cooperative and adds essentially no new concerns beyond divulging recipient preferences, since intermediaries already convert on their own initiative. It points to RFC 3238 for the wider discussion of intermediaries.
sections.eli5: Telling the mail system what your device can read reveals a little about you. And a mail worker who rewrites letters could break a sealed or signed letter, or get overworked.

data.title: Content-Previous
data.code:
Content-Previous:
   Date  Tue, 1 Jul 2001 10:52:37 +0200;
   By    relay.example.com;
   (&(image-file-structure=TIFF-minimal)
     (MRC-mode=0)
     (color=Binary)
     (&(dpi=400)
       (dpi-xyratio=1) )
     (&(image-coding=JBIG)
       (image-coding-constraint=JBIG-T85)
       (JBIG-stripe-size=128) )
     (size-x=2150/254)
     (paper-size=A4)
     (ua-media=stationery) )
